t.1.87.1: But which of these two first attains oneness with the gods, O king, when both are racing onward like the sun and the moon?
t.1.87.2: Yayāti said: Homeless though among householders, self-restrained though among those who live by desire, the mendicant who dwells in the very village has gone ahead of those two.
t.1.87.3: But if one who has not attained a long life should, once he has reached that state, fall into wrongdoing, and after doing it feels remorse, he should then undertake a further austerity.
t.1.87.4: What is cruel, that they call unwholesome. He who practises dharma with no thought of gain, even though he is without wealth and likewise without power, O king: that is uprightness, he is composure itself, that is noble.
t.1.87.5: By whom have you been sent here today as a messenger, O king, you who are young, garlanded, handsome and radiant? From where have you come, and from which direction, or do you have some abode on earth?
t.1.87.6: My merit exhausted, cast down from the sky to enter this earthly hell, the earth, I shall fall at once once I have spoken to you; the brahmins, the guardians of the worlds, are hurrying me on.
t.1.87.8: I ask you, O king, do not fall the fall: if there are worlds for me here, whether situated in the mid-air or in heaven, tell me, for I deem you a knower of that law.
t.1.87.7: But I chose my fall into the presence of the good, and these here gathered are all men of virtue. For this boon I obtained from Śakra as I was about to fall to the surface of the earth, O lord of men.
t.1.87.10: Those worlds that are mine in heaven, O lord of kings, I give to you; do not fall headlong in your fall! Whether they rest in the mid-air or in heaven, ascend to them swiftly, O vanquisher of foes.
t.1.87.9: As many as are the cattle and horses found upon the earth, together with the wild beasts and the mountains, so many are those worlds established in heaven. Know it thus, O lion among kings.
t.1.87.11: One such as I, who is not a brāhmaṇa yet knows the brahman, does not engage in accepting gifts, O foremost of kings. Just as one ought always to give to the twice-born, so did I give in former times, O lord of men.
t.1.87.13: I, Pratardana, ask you, O you of enviable form: are there worlds for me, whether situated in the mid-air or in heaven? I consider you a knower of the field of that dharma.
t.1.87.12: One who is not a brahmin should never live as a beggar, nor should a brahmin woman who is the wife of a hero. So if I were to do what has never been done before, seeking to gain something, what good would there be in that?
t.1.87.15: Those I give to you; do not fall the fall. Whatever worlds are mine, let them indeed be yours, whether they rest in the mid-air or in heaven; step onto them swiftly, freed from your bewilderment.
t.1.87.14: Many are those worlds, lord of men, each one even of seven times seven days; dripping with honey, mingled with ghee, free from sorrow, they are without end, and they await you.
t.1.87.16: One of equal splendour should not covet merit or security as a gift, O king, while he himself is a king; a wise king, even when he has met misfortune by the decree of fate, should never act basely.
t.1.87.17: A king who reflects on a path that is righteous and brings glory should act with his eyes on dharma. No one like me, whose mind is set on dharma, would knowingly do so wretched a thing as you propose to me.
t.1.87.18: "Should I do something unprecedented, something never done by others, when I seek to know what is right in this matter?" To King Yayāti, who spoke thus, Vasumanas, best of kings, said:
